MODULE_GOAL: Build and analyze simple circuits; connect gates to matrices/rotations.

LEARNING_OBJECTIVES: Identify the parts of a quantum circuit diagram: wires (qubit registers), gates, and measurement symbols.
Explain the left-to-right time-flow convention used in circuit diagrams.
Explain why a measurement operation is typically drawn at the end of a circuit and what it outputs.
Explain why every quantum gate box must have the same number of wires entering and exiting it (reversibility).
SUBTOPICS.CORE_EXPLANATION:
A quantum circuit diagram is a picture that describes a sequence of operations applied to one or more qubits. Each qubit register is drawn as a horizontal line, or wire, with the top line usually labeled qubit 0, the next line qubit 1, and so on. Quantum operations are drawn as boxes placed on these wires, called quantum gates, in direct analogy to classical logic gates. Crucially, time flows from left to right in a circuit diagram: the left-most gate on a wire is the one applied first, and gates further to the right are applied later, in chronological order. The wires entering a gate box represent the qubit(s) going into that operation, and the wires leaving it represent the qubit(s) coming out.

Because every quantum operation on qubits (other than measurement) must be reversible — a consequence of the fact that quantum operations are represented by unitary matrices — any gate box drawn in a circuit must have exactly the same number of wires entering it as exiting it. If a gate had more outputs than inputs, information would have to be created from nothing, which would break reversibility and therefore couldn't correspond to a valid unitary operation. Measurement is the one operation in a circuit that is not reversible and not unitary: it is drawn using a distinctive meter symbol, takes a qubit register (a solid wire) as input, and produces classical information (conventionally drawn as a double line) as output. Because measurement irreversibly collapses the qubit's quantum state into a definite classical result, it is almost always placed at the very end of a circuit, after all the reversible gate operations have been applied, so useful quantum information isn't collapsed prematurely.
SUBTOPICS.MATHEMATICAL_REPRESENTATION: Circuit reading order vs matrix order: a circuit applying gate A, then B, then C (left to right) corresponds to the matrix product CBA applied to the initial state — i.e. |output⟩ = CBA|input⟩ (matrix multiplication is applied right-to-left, the OPPOSITE order from how gates are read in the diagram).
SUBTOPICS.INTUITION_ANALOGY: Think of a circuit diagram like sheet music read left to right: each gate is a note played in order, and the wire is the instrument's string carrying the qubit through time. The measurement symbol at the end is like the final note being recorded — once it's played (measured), you can't take it back or replay a different version; that's why it's saved for last.

EXAMPLES.MATRIX_FORM: Final state (before measurement) = X·H·|0⟩ (matrix multiplication applied right to left)

EXAMPLES.EXPLANATION: A single-qubit gate box has exactly 1 wire in and 1 wire out, because it represents a 2x2 unitary matrix acting on a 2-dimensional state vector — the number of qubits (and thus dimensions) is preserved.

SUBTOPICS.CONCEPT: Standard Gate Set (Pauli X/Y/Z, H, S, T)
PREREQUISITES: Matrices and matrix multiplication (basic linear algebra)
LEARNING_OBJECTIVES: Write out the 2x2 matrices for the Pauli X, Y, Z gates, the Hadamard (H) gate, the phase (S) gate, and the T gate.
Explain that single-qubit quantum operations are represented by 2x2 unitary matrices.
Compute the result of applying any of these gates to a given single-qubit state vector.
Recognize the T gate as the standard non-Clifford gate and S = T².
SUBTOPICS.CORE_EXPLANATION:
In quantum computing, operations on qubits are represented by square matrices. Since a single qubit's state is a 2-dimensional column vector, single-qubit operations are represented by 2×2 matrices. A quantum operation must be a unitary matrix U, meaning UU† = U†U = 𝕀 (its adjoint, or conjugate transpose, equals its inverse); this property guarantees that applying the operation preserves the norm of the state vector, so the result is always still a valid, properly normalized quantum state.

The standard single-qubit gate set consists of the Pauli operators X, Y, and Z; the Hadamard gate H; the phase gate S; and the T gate. X = [[0,1],[1,0]] swaps the amplitudes of |0⟩ and |1⟩ (a bit flip). Z = [[1,0],[0,-1]] leaves |0⟩ unchanged but flips the sign of |1⟩'s amplitude (a phase flip). Y = [[0,-i],[i,0]] combines both a bit flip and a phase flip. H = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,-1]] turns a basis state into an equal superposition (or vice versa). S = [[1,0],[0,i]] applies a quarter-turn phase to the |1⟩ amplitude, and is related to T by S = T². T = [[1,0],[0,e^(iπ/4)]] (also called the π/8 gate) applies a smaller, one-eighth-turn phase to the |1⟩ amplitude and is the standard non-Clifford gate; X, Y, Z, H, and S are collectively called the Clifford gates. Together, the Clifford gates plus T form a set that can approximate any single-qubit unitary transformation, which is why this particular gate set is used as the standard building-block vocabulary for single-qubit circuits.
SUBTOPICS.INTUITION_ANALOGY: Think of these six gates as a small toolbox of standard moves: X is a 'swap' tool (flip 0 and 1), Z is a 'sign-flip' tool that only touches the |1⟩ part, Y does both at once, H is the 'mixer' that turns a definite state into a blend (or unmixes a blend back to definite), and S and T are 'fine-adjustment' tools that nudge the phase of the |1⟩ part by a quarter-turn and an eighth-turn respectively. Just like a small set of screwdriver bits can tackle almost any screw, this small gate set (plus enough repetition) can approximate almost any single-qubit operation.

EXAMPLES.DESCRIPTION: Applying S then T to |1⟩ (accumulating phase)
EXAMPLES.RESULT: S|1⟩ = i|1⟩; then T(i|1⟩) = i·e^(iπ/4)|1⟩ — phases accumulate multiplicatively

VISUALIZATIONS: Table listing each gate's name, matrix, and one-line effect (X: bit flip, Z: phase flip, H: mixer, S/T: fine phase adjustments)
Bar chart comparing |0⟩/|1⟩ measurement probabilities before and after each gate is applied to a sample state
Circuit snippets for each gate showing before/after statevectors
COMMON_MISCONCEPTIONS: Not all 2x2 matrices are valid quantum gates — only unitary matrices (U U† = 𝕀) are.
S and T are related but not identical: S = T², so two T gates in a row equal one S gate.
The Y gate is not simply 'X then Z' as plain matrix addition — it is its own distinct unitary matrix combining a bit flip and phase flip with a specific complex structure ([[0,-i],[i,0]]).

LEARNING_OBJECTIVES: Explain how applying gates sequentially in a circuit corresponds to multiplying their matrices together.
Correctly order matrix multiplication given a sequence of gates read left to right in a circuit diagram.
Define a unitary matrix and explain why quantum gates must be unitary.
Compute the overall matrix (and resulting state vector) for a short sequence of single-qubit gates.
SUBTOPICS.CORE_EXPLANATION:
Multiplying two matrices M (size m×n) and N (size n×p) produces a new matrix P (size m×p), where each entry P_ik is the sum over j of M_ij · N_jk — equivalently, entry P_11 is the scalar (dot) product of the first row of M with the first column of N, and so on for every entry. Because a vector is just a special case of a matrix (with only one column), this same rule defines how a matrix acts on a state vector: applying gate matrix G to state vector |ψ⟩ is simply the matrix-vector product G|ψ⟩.

When several gates are applied one after another in a circuit, the overall effect is found by multiplying their matrices together — but the order matters and can be a common source of confusion. In a circuit diagram, gates are read left to right in the order they are applied over time. In matrix notation, however, matrix multiplication is applied right to left: the matrix closest to the state vector acts first. So a circuit that applies gate A, then B, then C corresponds to the overall matrix CBA, applied to the input state as CBA|ψ⟩ — A is written last (closest to |ψ⟩) precisely because it's applied first.

A special square matrix is the identity matrix 𝕀 (all 1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere), which leaves any vector unchanged. For a square matrix A, a matrix B is its inverse if AB = BA = 𝕀, and quantum operations must specifically be unitary matrices: a matrix U is unitary if U U† = U† U = 𝕀, i.e., its inverse equals its own adjoint (conjugate transpose). This unitarity requirement is what guarantees that the norm of the state vector — and therefore the total measurement probability of 1 — is preserved after every single gate in the circuit, and therefore after the entire sequence of gates as well, since a product of unitary matrices is itself always unitary.
SUBTOPICS.MATHEMATICAL_REPRESENTATION:
Matrix multiplication: P = MN, with entries P_ik = Σ_j M_ij N_jk
Circuit → matrix translation: circuit applies A, then B, then C (left to right)  ⇒  final state = CBA|ψ⟩
Unitary condition: U U† = U† U = 𝕀  (equivalently, U⁻¹ = U†)
Product of unitaries is unitary: if U and V are unitary, then UV is also unitary
SUBTOPICS.INTUITION_ANALOGY: Composing gates is like following a recipe written on index cards, laid out left to right on a table (the circuit), but you have to physically fold the cards into a single stack to cook (the matrix), and the bottom card in the stack — the one your hands touch first — is the first step. So the recipe you read left-to-right ends up stacked right-to-left when written as a single combined instruction (the matrix product).

EXAMPLES.DESCRIPTION: Composing H then Z then H, written correctly as matrices
EXAMPLES.MATRIX_ORDER: Final state = H · Z · H · |0⟩  (H applied first is written right-most, closest to |0⟩)

EXAMPLES.RESULT: H is confirmed to be unitary, since H H† = 𝕀

EXAMPLES.DESCRIPTION: Order matters: XZ vs ZX applied to |1⟩
EXAMPLES.XZ_ORDER: Circuit: Z then X (Z applied first) ⇒ matrix X·Z|1⟩ = X(-|1⟩) = -|0⟩
EXAMPLES.ZX_ORDER: Circuit: X then Z (X applied first) ⇒ matrix Z·X|1⟩ = Z(|0⟩) = |0⟩
EXAMPLES.RESULT: The two circuits give results differing by a global phase (−1) in this case, illustrating that gate order can change the outcome and must be tracked carefully

VISUALIZATIONS: Step-by-step matrix multiplication grid showing how each output entry is a dot product of a row and column
Circuit-to-matrix-expression translator diagram, showing the left-to-right vs right-to-left order flip
Animated stacking of gate matrices building up the overall circuit unitary
COMMON_MISCONCEPTIONS: The order of gates in a circuit (left to right, applied in that order) is NOT the same as the left-to-right order of matrices when you write the product — the matrices are multiplied in reverse (right to left) order.
Gate composition is not commutative in general: applying gate A then B is not always the same as applying B then A.
A sequence of unitary gates always produces an overall unitary transformation — the state remains validly normalized throughout the whole circuit, not just after each individual gate.

MCQS.QUESTION: A circuit applies H, then Z, then H to |0⟩ (left to right). What is the correctly ordered matrix product for the final state, and what is the result?

LEARNING_OBJECTIVES: Design a one-gate circuit that creates an equal superposition from |0⟩.
Design a one-gate circuit that flips |0⟩ to |1⟩ (or vice versa).
Compute the final state vector for a short sequence of gates applied to |0⟩.
Describe, at a light conceptual level, what 'phase kickback' means in a controlled-gate setting.
SUBTOPICS.CORE_EXPLANATION:
With just a handful of standard gates, you can already build several important and reusable single-qubit circuit patterns. The most fundamental 'superposition-creating' pattern is a single Hadamard gate applied to |0⟩: H|0⟩ = |+⟩ = (1/√2)(|0⟩ + |1⟩), producing a qubit that measures 0 or 1 with equal (50/50) probability. The most fundamental 'state-flipping' pattern is a single Pauli X gate, which swaps the amplitudes of |0⟩ and |1⟩ — X|0⟩ = |1⟩ and X|1⟩ = |0⟩ — acting as a quantum bit-flip. These two one-gate patterns, along with combinations like applying Z after H to flip the relative phase of a superposition, form the basic vocabulary used to prepare a wide range of target single-qubit states starting from |0⟩.

A more advanced (but conceptually important) pattern involves controlled gates, where a target qubit's operation is applied conditionally on a separate control qubit's value: Λ(G)(α|0⟩+β|1⟩)|ψ⟩ = α|0⟩|ψ⟩ + β|1⟩G|ψ⟩ — meaning the operation G is applied to the target only in the branch where the control qubit is |1⟩. A subtle and useful effect called phase kickback can occur here: if the target qubit |ψ⟩ happens to be an eigenstate of G with eigenvalue e^(iφ) (so that G|ψ⟩ = e^(iφ)|ψ⟩), then that phase factor doesn't stay hidden on the target — it gets 'kicked back' onto the control qubit instead, turning the control's superposition α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ into α|0⟩ + β e^(iφ)|1⟩|ψ⟩, i.e. a relative phase appears on the control. This module only introduces the intuition at a light level, since phase kickback truly comes alive once multi-qubit and controlled circuits are studied in depth in a later module — here it's enough to recognize that a phase acquired by a target qubit under a controlled operation can 'leak back' to affect the control qubit's own relative phase.
SUBTOPICS.MATHEMATICAL_REPRESENTATION:
Superposition pattern: H|0⟩ = (1/√2)(|0⟩ + |1⟩) = |+⟩
Flip pattern: X|0⟩ = |1⟩,  X|1⟩ = |0⟩
Phase-flip-on-superposition pattern: Z·H|0⟩ = Z|+⟩ = (1/√2)(|0⟩ − |1⟩) = |−⟩
Controlled-gate action: Λ(G)(α|0⟩ + β|1⟩)|ψ⟩ = α|0⟩|ψ⟩ + β|1⟩ G|ψ⟩
Phase kickback (light intuition): if G|ψ⟩ = e^(iφ)|ψ⟩, then Λ(G)(α|0⟩+β|1⟩)|ψ⟩ = (α|0⟩ + β e^(iφ)|1⟩)|ψ⟩
SUBTOPICS.INTUITION_ANALOGY: Preparing states from |0⟩ with gates is like starting from a blank page and applying a small set of stamps in sequence to reach a target picture: one Hadamard stamp gives you an even 'blend' (superposition), one X stamp flips the page over completely, and stacking an X and Z stamp in different combinations gives you |+⟩, |−⟩, |0⟩, or |1⟩ depending on the order. Phase kickback is stranger: imagine flipping a coin (the target) whose result secretly depends on another coin (the control) — if flipping the target coin doesn't actually change which face it shows (it's already 'settled', like an eigenstate) but does leave an invisible mark, that mark ends up appearing on the control coin instead, even though nothing about the control coin's physical face changed.

Design a circuit to prepare |1⟩ from |0⟩
Design a circuit to prepare |−⟩ from |0⟩
EXAMPLES.EXPECTED_SIMULATION: Measurement histogram over many shots ~ 50% |0⟩, 50% |1⟩ (same probabilities as |+⟩, but a different relative phase)

EXAMPLES.DESCRIPTION: Light phase-kickback intuition with a controlled-Z-like gate
EXAMPLES.SETUP: Control qubit in state |+⟩ = (1/√2)(|0⟩+|1⟩); target qubit |ψ⟩ is an eigenstate of G with eigenvalue -1 (i.e., G|ψ⟩ = -|ψ⟩)
EXAMPLES.RESULT: Λ(G)|+⟩|ψ⟩ = (1/√2)(|0⟩|ψ⟩ - |1⟩|ψ⟩) = |−⟩|ψ⟩ — the -1 phase from G acting on the target has 'kicked back' onto the control qubit, turning |+⟩ into |−⟩

VISUALIZATIONS: Bloch sphere before/after diagram for H|0⟩ → |+⟩ and X|0⟩ → |1⟩

Simple schematic of the phase-kickback setup: control qubit, target qubit, controlled-G box, with an arrow showing the phase 'jumping back' to the control
COMMON_MISCONCEPTIONS: Different circuits can produce states with identical measurement probabilities (like |+⟩ and |−⟩) yet still be physically different states due to relative phase — always track the full state vector, not just probabilities.
Phase kickback does not change the target qubit's own state or probabilities at all — the entire observable effect lands on the control qubit's relative phase.
There is often more than one valid circuit to prepare a given target state — e.g., a global phase or an alternate gate sequence can reach the 'same' physical state in more than one way.
